standard.title: Evaluate civic participation methods
standard.description: evaluate the methods or strategies related to making decisions about civic participation
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can explain the methods or strategies related to making decisions about civic participation (AC9HC8S04). At Year 9 the expectation advances from explaining to evaluating — students must assess whether methods are effective and what their intended and unintended effects are.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students evaluate the methods or strategies used in civic participation decisions, assess intended and unintended effects of action plans, and develop evaluated plans for addressing a contemporary civic issue.

nodes.label: Examining civic action plans
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can examine a government or community action plan, identifying its actions, measures, and intended and unintended effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Examine one government or community action plan and identify its intended goals and at least one measure used to achieve them.
nodes.typical_width: Examine a government action plan and identify the actions, the measures, and the intended and unintended effects of the plan; use examples such as a local recycling program, a national literacy campaign, or a waste reduction strategy; explain how intended and unintended effects are discovered and how they should inform future planning.
wider: Compare two civic action plans on the same issue (e.g. two different government approaches to reducing plastic waste) and evaluate which methods were more effective and why
Investigate how a government action plan has been evaluated over time and assess whether evaluation data led to changes in method
Examine an action plan that produced significant unintended negative effects and analyse what evaluation processes could have identified the risk earlier
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to identify actions, measures, and effects is prerequisite to developing an evaluated plan in Node 2. Students who cannot distinguish a measure (how progress is tracked) from an action (what is done) cannot build evaluation criteria into their own planning.

response_modes.reason: Students frequently conflate 'what we will do' with 'how we will know it worked'. An explicit scaffold that separates action → measure → intended effect → evaluation builds the analytical vocabulary needed for Node 2's planning work.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two specific actions in a civic action plan
Identifies at least one intended effect and one measure used to track it

nodes.label: Developing and evaluating a civic participation plan
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can develop a plan to address a contemporary civic issue that incorporates a consultation process and evaluation criteria.
nodes.minimum_width: Develop a basic plan to address a civic issue that includes at least one action, one measure of success, and one way to consult stakeholders.
nodes.typical_width: Develop a plan of action to address a contemporary civic issue that incorporates a consultation process to ensure a range of views are heard, and participants are provided with opportunities to contribute; include evaluation criteria for assessing effectiveness; consider examples such as a local safety campaign, a community sustainability initiative, or an educational resources strategy.
wider: Develop and peer-review plans for addressing the same civic issue using different methods (e.g. media campaign vs community consultation vs policy advocacy) and evaluate which approach best fits the context
Evaluate government media campaigns and community activities used over time to address a recurring civic issue (e.g. littering, road safety) and determine which have been most effective and why
Incorporate feedback loops into a civic plan — specifying how the plan would be revised if early evaluation data indicated it was not working

response_modes.reason: Developing a plan integrates the analytical skills from Node 1 (examining existing plans) with the capability skills of civic planning. Students are executing a genuine mode B task — the thinking is only legible through the plan they produce.

Plans developed for contrasting civic contexts (a local personal safety issue, an international development or aid context) build transferability — students learn that civic planning methods must be adapted to context, not just applied formulaically.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Civic planning is a genuinely generative capability. Advancing students who develop plans for multiple civic contexts across different scales and stakeholder groups are building transferable skills in consultation design, evaluation, and advocacy — relevant well beyond the Year 9 curriculum.
success_criteria: Develops a plan that includes at least one action, one consultation mechanism, and one evaluation criterion
Explains how the consultation process ensures a range of views will be represented
